Ex Q.1 (E):
The chapter's rules are that the more important (more stable) resonance structure is the one with (a) more covalent bonds, (b) more atoms carrying a complete octet, (c) less separation of opposite charges, and (d) any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.

a. The **first** structure, \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(=O)-\overset{\bullet\bullet}{O}H}\), is more favourable. It has one more covalent bond than the second, every atom in it has a complete octet, and it carries no charges at all, whereas the second structure separates a negative charge on to one oxygen and a positive charge on to the other. Charge separation always costs energy, so the uncharged structure contributes more to the hybrid.

b. The **first** structure, \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}H_2-CH=CH-O^{\ominus}}\), is more favourable. Both structures have the same number of covalent bonds and the same degree of charge separation, so the deciding rule is (d) : here the negative charge sits on oxygen, which is the more electronegative atom, and the positive charge on carbon, which is the more electropositive. In the second structure the charges are the wrong way round — a negative charge on carbon and a positive charge on oxygen — which is much less favourable.

Ex Q.1 (G):
[Textbook note (not an error): part (c) has no unambiguous answer at the level this chapter develops. The chapter teaches that a halogen exerts a -I effect, which destabilises a carbocation and makes \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}H_3}\) the most stable of the three — the answer given, and the one that makes part (c) the exact mirror of part (b). The same chapter also teaches that a halogen has lone pairs and can show a +R effect, which acting alone would stabilise a chlorine-bearing carbocation and reverse the order. The chapter never weighs the two effects against each other for a halogen bonded directly to the positive carbon.]

a. The three species are free radicals : methyl, isopropyl (secondary) and tert-butyl (tertiary). Alkyl groups release electrons (+I effect) and, more importantly, each \(\alpha\) C-H bond can delocalise its \(\sigma\) electrons into the half-filled p orbital (hyperconjugation). The tertiary radical \(\mathrm{CH_3-\underset{CH_3}{\overset{\bullet}{C}}-CH_3}\) has three \(\alpha\)-methyl groups and so nine \(\alpha\)-hydrogens, against six for the isopropyl radical and none for the methyl radical. The chapter's order is tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl, so the **tert-butyl free radical is the most stable**.

b. The three species are carbanions, which carry a negative charge on carbon. A negative charge is stabilised by groups that **withdraw** electrons. Bromine is more electronegative than carbon and exerts a -I effect, and the effect adds up with the number of bromine atoms. \(\mathrm{\overset{\ominus}{C}Br_3}\) has three of them, so it disperses the negative charge best and is the **most stable**. \(\mathrm{\overset{\ominus}{C}H_3}\), with no electron-withdrawing group at all, is the least stable of the three.

c. The three species are carbanions' opposite, carbocations, which carry a positive charge on carbon. A positive charge is stabilised by groups that **release** electrons and destabilised by groups that withdraw them. Chlorine exerts a -I effect, and it grows with the number of chlorine atoms, so on the inductive argument the chapter develops, \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}H_3}\) — the one carrying no chlorine — is the **most stable** and \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}Cl_3}\) the least.
Ex Q.1 (H):
The \(\alpha\)-carbon is the carbon atom **directly attached** to the reactive centre — here the positively charged carbon, or the doubly bonded carbon. The \(\alpha\)-hydrogens are the hydrogens carried by those \(\alpha\)-carbons.

a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-\overset{\oplus}{C}H-CH_2-CH_3}\). The charged carbon is the middle one, so the \(\alpha\)-carbons are the **two \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) groups** flanking it. Each carries 2 hydrogens, so the total number of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens is \(2 + 2 = 4\).

b. \(\mathrm{H_3C-\overset{\oplus}{C}(C_6H_{11})-CH_2-CH_3}\), where \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}}\) is the cyclohexyl ring drawn below the charged carbon. Three carbons are attached to the charged carbon, so all three are \(\alpha\)-carbons : **the \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) group, the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) of the ethyl group, and the ring carbon** joined to it. They carry 3, 2 and 1 hydrogens respectively, so the total number of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens is \(3 + 2 + 1 = 6\).

c. \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_3}\). Here the reactive centre is the C = C double bond, and the only \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) carbon attached to it is the **third carbon, the \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) group**. That is the single \(\alpha\)-carbon, and it carries 2 hydrogens, so the total number of \(\alpha\)-hydrogens is 2.
Ex Q.1 (I):
A saturated carbon is classified by the number of **other carbon atoms** bonded to it : one makes it primary (\(1^\circ\)), two secondary (\(2^\circ\)), three tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) and four quaternary (\(4^\circ\)).

a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\), that is 2,2,3-trimethylhexane, which has nine carbon atoms in all.

- **Quaternary (1) :** C-2, which is bonded to C-1, to C-3 and to its two methyl groups — four carbons.
- **Tertiary (1) :** C-3, which is bonded to C-2, to C-4 and to one methyl group — three carbons.
- **Secondary (2) :** C-4 and C-5, each bonded to two carbons.
- **Primary (5) :** C-1, C-6 and the three methyl branches (two on C-2, one on C-3), each bonded to only one carbon.

The four counts add to \(1 + 1 + 2 + 5 = 9\), which is the total number of carbons, as it must be.

b. The bicyclic hydrocarbon drawn is bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane, seven carbons in two fused rings sharing a one-carbon bridge.

- **Tertiary (2) :** the two **bridgehead** carbons, each joined to three other carbons.
- **Secondary (5) :** the remaining five \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) carbons — four in the ring and the one bridging carbon — each joined to two others.
- **Primary (0)** and **quaternary (0)** : there is no \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) group anywhere in the molecule and no carbon joined to four other carbons.

Again the counts add to \(2 + 5 = 7\), the total number of carbons.
Ex Q.2:
| Column 'A' | Column 'B' |
|---|---|
| i. Inductive effect | d. displacement of \(\sigma\) electrons |
| ii. Hyperconjugation | c. delocalisation of \(\sigma\) electrons |
| iii. Resonance effect | a. delocalisation of \(\pi\) electrons |

The inductive effect is a **displacement** — the shared pair of a \(\sigma\) bond is pulled towards the more electronegative atom but stays in that bond, so it is only polarised, never spread over several atoms. Hyperconjugation genuinely **delocalises** the \(\sigma\) electrons of an \(\alpha\) C-H bond into an adjacent p orbital or \(\pi\) system, which is why the chapter calls it 'no bond resonance'. The resonance effect **delocalises \(\pi\) electrons** (or a lone pair) over a conjugated system. The unused entry, 'b. displacement of \(\pi\) electrons', describes the electromeric effect, which is temporary and appears only in the presence of an attacking reagent.
Ex Q.3:
A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds that all contain the same functional group and can be represented by one general molecular formula. Successive members differ by a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) unit, so their molecular masses differ by 14, they are all made by similar methods and they show a graded change in physical properties with a very similar chemical behaviour. Each member of such a series is called a homologue of the others.

A. Starting from \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) the series is that of the **aldehydes**. Its first four members from this point are

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) (ethanal, \(\mathrm{C_2H_4O}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\) (propanal, \(\mathrm{C_3H_6O}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO}\) (butanal, \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CHO}\) (pentanal, \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\)).

General molecular formula : \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}O}\), which may also be written \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+1}CHO}\).

B. Starting from \(\mathrm{H-C\equiv C-H}\) the series is that of the **alkynes**. Its first four members are

\(\mathrm{HC\equiv CH}\) (ethyne, \(\mathrm{C_2H_2}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3-C\equiv CH}\) (propyne, \(\mathrm{C_3H_4}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C\equiv CH}\) (but-1-yne, \(\mathrm{C_4H_6}\)), \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-C\equiv CH}\) (pent-1-yne, \(\mathrm{C_5H_8}\)).

General molecular formula : \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n-2}}\).

Ex Q.6 (A):
In phenol the oxygen of the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group carries lone pairs in a p orbital that overlaps the \(\pi\) system of the ring, so a lone pair can be delocalised into the ring. This is the +R effect, and it raises the electron density at the **ortho** and **para** positions.

Four resonance structures can be written.

**I** — the ordinary uncharged structure : the benzene ring with alternating double bonds and an \(\mathrm{-\overset{\bullet\bullet}{O}H}\) group on C-1. No charges anywhere.

**II** — a lone pair on oxygen forms a second bond to C-1, giving \(\mathrm{=\overset{\oplus}{O}H}\); the \(\pi\) pair that was between C-1 and C-2 moves on to C-2, which therefore carries the negative charge. So the oxygen is positive and the **ortho** carbon negative.

**III** — the same, but the negative charge ends up on C-4, the **para** carbon.

**IV** — the same, but the negative charge ends up on C-6, the other **ortho** carbon.

All four are joined by double-headed arrows. Structure I, being uncharged and having every atom with a complete octet, is the most stable and contributes most to the hybrid; II, III and IV involve charge separation and contribute less, but they are what make the ortho and para positions of phenol electron rich.
Ex Q.6 (B):
In benzaldehyde the \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group is attached to the ring and its \(\mathrm{C=O}\) is conjugated with the ring \(\pi\) system. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the group **withdraws** \(\pi\) electrons from the ring : this is the -R effect, and it leaves a positive charge at the **ortho** and **para** positions.

Four resonance structures can be written.

**I** — the ordinary uncharged structure : the benzene ring with alternating double bonds and \(\mathrm{-C(=O)-H}\) on C-1. No charges anywhere.

**II** — the \(\pi\) pair of the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) shifts entirely on to the oxygen, which becomes \(\mathrm{-\overset{\bullet\bullet}{O}{}^{\ominus}}\); a ring \(\pi\) pair then moves to form a double bond between C-1 and the carbonyl carbon, leaving C-2 short of electrons. The oxygen is negative and the **ortho** carbon positive.

**III** — the same, but the positive charge ends up on C-4, the **para** carbon.

**IV** — the same, but the positive charge ends up on C-6, the other **ortho** carbon.

Structure I contributes most, since it carries no charge separation and every atom has a complete octet. Structures II, III and IV are why the ring in benzaldehyde is electron poor at the ortho and para positions, the opposite of what happens in phenol.
Ex Q.6 (C):
Buta-1,3-diene has two \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bonds separated by a single \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond, which is a conjugated system, so resonance structures can be written by shifting the \(\pi\) electrons.

\(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH=CH_2}\) (I) \(\longleftrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}H_2-CH=CH-\overset{\ominus}{C}H_2}\) (II) \(\longleftrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{\overset{\ominus}{C}H_2-CH=CH-\overset{\oplus}{C}H_2}\) (III)

In II the \(\pi\) pair of the first double bond moves to C-2-C-3, so C-1 is left electron deficient and C-4 electron rich; III is the mirror image of II with the charges the other way round.

Structure I is the most stable and contributes most : it has one more covalent bond than II or III, every carbon has a complete octet, and there is no separation of charge. II and III are equivalent to each other and contribute equally but much less. Their existence is what gives the central \(\mathrm{C_2-C_3}\) bond some double bond character and makes the molecule resonance stabilised.
Ex Q.6 (D):
The acetate ion is \(\mathrm{CH_3-COO^{\ominus}}\). The negative charge sits on one oxygen while the other is doubly bonded to the same carbon, and that oxygen's lone pair is in a p orbital conjugated with the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) \(\pi\) bond, so two resonance structures can be written.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C(=O)-O^{\ominus}}\) (I) \(\longleftrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(-O^{\ominus})=O}\) (II)

The two structures are **equivalent** to each other — each has the same number of covalent bonds, the same atoms with complete octets and the negative charge on an oxygen — so they contribute equally to the hybrid. The chapter's rule is that when all the resonance structures of a species are equivalent, the species is highly resonance stabilised, and the acetate ion is exactly such a case. In the real ion the negative charge is shared equally between the two oxygens and both carbon-oxygen bonds are identical.
Ex Q.7 (A):
| Inductive effect | Resonance effect |
|---|---|
| It is the **displacement** of the shared electron pair of a \(\sigma\) bond towards the more electronegative atom. | It is the **delocalisation** of \(\pi\) electrons, or of a lone pair on an atom attached to a \(\pi\) bond, over a conjugated system. |
| It is transmitted through \(\sigma\) bonds. | It is transmitted through a chain of conjugated \(\pi\) bonds. |
| The electrons are only polarised; they stay within the bond and no new structures are written. | The electrons are actually spread over several atoms, and the species is described by two or more resonance structures joined by double-headed arrows. |
| Its magnitude falls off sharply along the chain and is negligible beyond about three carbon atoms. | It operates over the whole conjugated system without such rapid weakening. |
| It is classified as -I (electron withdrawing, e.g. \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\)) or +I (electron releasing, e.g. alkyl groups). | It is classified as -R (electron withdrawing, e.g. \(\mathrm{-CHO}\), \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\)) or +R (electron releasing, e.g. \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), halogen). |

Both are permanent electronic effects present in the ground state of the molecule.

Ex Q.8 (A):
**False.**

Corrected statement : Homolytic fission involves **symmetrical** breaking of a covalent bond.

In homolysis the two electrons of the shared pair are divided equally, one going to each of the bonded atoms, so two neutral free radicals are produced. Unsymmetrical breaking, in which both electrons go to one atom, is heterolytic fission.
Ex Q.8 (B):
**False.**

Corrected statement : Heterolytic fission results in the formation of **ions — a cation and an anion**. (Alternatively : **Homolytic** fission results in the formation of free radicals.)

In heterolysis both electrons of the shared pair go to the more electronegative of the two bonded atoms, so that atom becomes negatively charged and the other positively charged. Free radicals, which are neutral species carrying an unpaired electron, come from homolysis.
Ex Q.8 (C):
**False.**

Corrected statement : Free radicals are **neutral** species carrying one unpaired electron.

A free radical is formed when a covalent bond breaks symmetrically, so each fragment keeps one of the two shared electrons and neither gains nor loses charge. It is highly reactive because it seeks one more electron to pair with, but it carries no charge. A negatively charged carbon species is a carbanion, not a free radical.
Ex Q.8 (D):
**False.**

Corrected statement : Aniline is a **homocyclic (carbocyclic) aromatic** compound.

A heterocyclic compound is one in which the **ring itself** contains at least one atom other than carbon, such as pyridine, pyrrole, furan or thiophene. In aniline the ring is a benzene ring made entirely of carbon atoms; the nitrogen is in the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group attached to the ring, outside it. Aniline is therefore benzenoid aromatic and carbocyclic.
Ex Q.9:
Phytane is 2,6,10,14-tetramethylhexadecane, so its skeleton is a straight chain of **sixteen** carbon atoms carrying a methyl group on C-2, C-6, C-10 and C-14. That makes twenty carbon atoms in all, and the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_{20}H_{42}}\).

**Zig-zag (bond line) formula :** draw a continuous zig-zag of fifteen line segments, which gives sixteen carbon points. Counting from the left-hand end, draw a short line out from the 2nd, 6th, 10th and 14th points, each representing one methyl branch. No C or H letters are written; every corner and both free ends are carbon atoms.

**Classification of the carbon atoms** (a carbon is primary, secondary, tertiary or quaternary according to whether it is bonded to one, two, three or four other carbons) :

- **Primary : 6** — the two chain ends C-1 and C-16, together with the four methyl branches.
- **Secondary : 10** — C-3, C-4, C-5, C-7, C-8, C-9, C-11, C-12, C-13 and C-15, each bonded to two other carbons.
- **Tertiary : 4** — C-2, C-6, C-10 and C-14, each bonded to two chain carbons plus its methyl branch.
- **Quaternary : 0** — no carbon in the molecule is bonded to four other carbons.

The counts add to \(6 + 10 + 4 + 0 = 20\), which is the total number of carbon atoms, as it must be.
Ex Q.10 (a):
Structure (i) is butanal, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CHO}\), and structure (ii) is 2-methylpropanal, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-CHO}\). What differs is the carbon skeleton : (i) has a straight chain of four carbons, while (ii) has a branched chain of three carbons carrying a methyl group.

Same molecular formula, same functional group, different carbon skeleton — the two are **chain isomers**, so the relation between them is chain isomerism.

Ex Q.11 (a):
Ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond of ethane **symmetrically**, one electron of the shared pair going to each carbon. Each fragment is therefore a neutral species carrying a single unpaired electron.

The reactive intermediate produced is the **methyl free radical**, \(\mathrm{\overset{\bullet}{C}H_3}\). Two of them are formed from each molecule of ethane. Because ultraviolet radiation favours homolytic fission, this is a free radical (non-polar) reaction.
Ex Q.11 (b):
The bond breaks homolytically, so the two electrons of the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bonding pair separate, one going to each carbon. The movement of a **single** electron is shown by a **half-headed curved arrow**, the 'fish hook', not by the full-headed arrow used for an electron pair.

Two fish hook arrows are therefore drawn from the middle of the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond, one curving to the left-hand carbon and one to the right-hand carbon. The tail of each arrow sits on the bond, showing where the electron comes from, and the head points at the atom the electron ends up on :

\(\mathrm{CH_3 \overset{\frown}{-} CH_3 \xrightarrow{\text{U. V. light}} \overset{\bullet}{C}H_3 + \overset{\bullet}{C}H_3}\)

where the arc drawn over the bond stands for the two half-headed arrows pointing outwards to the two carbon atoms.
Ex Q.11 (c):
The intermediate produced is the methyl free radical, \(\mathrm{\overset{\bullet}{C}H_3}\), and it is the **least stable** of the alkyl free radicals.

A free radical is stabilised by electron releasing alkyl groups on the radical carbon, both through their +I effect and, more importantly, through hyperconjugation — the delocalisation of the \(\sigma\) electrons of an \(\alpha\) C-H bond into the half filled p orbital. The methyl radical has **no \(\alpha\)-carbon at all**, so no such delocalisation is possible and no charge or electron deficiency can be dispersed. That is why the observed order runs tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl.

Being the least stabilised, the methyl radical is extremely reactive and has only a transitory existence : it immediately attacks another radical or molecule so as to pair its odd electron and restore a stable bonding pair. Its carbon is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised and the radical is planar trigonal, with the unpaired electron in the \(\mathrm{p_z}\) orbital.
Ex Q.12 (A):
The notation shows the electrons of each \(\sigma\) bond being pulled towards the chlorine atom : the arrowheads on the bonds point towards Cl, chlorine develops a small negative charge \(\delta\ominus\), and both carbons develop small positive charges \(\delta\oplus\).

The effect is the **inductive effect**, and because chlorine is more electronegative than carbon and withdraws electron density, it is specifically the **-I (electron withdrawing) inductive effect**.

Notice that the charge on the second carbon is smaller than that on the carbon bonded directly to chlorine : the effect is relayed from one \(\sigma\) bond to the next and dies away quickly along the chain, becoming negligible beyond about three carbon atoms.
Ex Q.12 (B):
The displacement shown is **permanent**.

The inductive effect arises simply from the difference in electronegativity between the two bonded atoms, so it is present in the **ground state** of the molecule all the time, whether or not any reagent is nearby. It is one of the two permanent electronic effects the chapter describes, the other being the resonance effect.

The electronic effect that is only **temporary** is the electromeric effect : there the \(\pi\) electron pair of a multiple bond is completely shifted to one of the doubly bonded atoms in the presence of an attacking reagent, and the shift disappears as soon as the reagent is removed.
Ex Q.13:
The isopropyl carbocation is \(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{\oplus}{C}H-CH_3}\). The positively charged carbon is \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridised and carries an **empty p orbital**, and the two methyl groups attached to it are \(\alpha\)-carbons. Each \(\alpha\) C-H bond whose \(\sigma\) electrons can align with that empty p orbital may be delocalised into it, and when they are, the hydrogen is left with **no bond** to the carbon — which is why these are called no-bond resonance structures.

Counting the \(\alpha\)-hydrogens : two methyl groups, three hydrogens each, gives **six \(\alpha\)-hydrogens**, so **six** no-bond resonance structures can be drawn, one for each of them. In every one of them the pattern is the same :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{\oplus}{C}H-CH_3} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{H^{\oplus}\ \ CH_2=CH-CH_3}\)

That is, the \(\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}\) double bond forms between the \(\alpha\)-carbon and the formerly positive carbon, and the hydrogen is written as \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) with no bond joining it to the carbon. The six structures differ only in **which** of the six \(\alpha\)-hydrogens has been detached — three from one methyl group and three from the other — together with the original structure, all linked by double-headed arrows.

Because more \(\alpha\)-hydrogens mean more no-bond resonance structures and hence greater dispersal of the positive charge, this is exactly why the tertiary carbocation \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\overset{\oplus}{C}}\), with nine \(\alpha\)-hydrogens, is more stable than this isopropyl cation with six.
Ex Q.14 (A):
tert-Butyl bromide is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br}\). Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so when the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond breaks heterolytically in a polar solvent, **both** electrons of the shared pair go to the bromine.

The anion produced is therefore the **bromide ion**, \(\mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\).

\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br \longrightarrow (CH_3)_3\overset{\oplus}{C} + Br^{\ominus}}\)
Ex Q.14 (B):
The bond breaking is **heterolytic fission (heterolysis)**.

The question itself states that the products are **ions**, and that is the defining outcome of heterolysis : both electrons of the shared pair go to one of the two bonded atoms, so one fragment ends up with a negative charge and the other with a positive charge. Homolysis, by contrast, splits the pair one electron each way and gives two neutral free radicals.

The conditions agree too — the chapter states that heterolysis is favoured in **polar solvents**, which is exactly what the question specifies. The movement of the electron pair is shown with a full-headed curved arrow running from the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond to the bromine.
Ex Q.14 (C):
The cation formed is the tert-butyl carbocation, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\overset{\oplus}{C}}\). Its geometry is **trigonal planar**.

When the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond breaks and the bromine leaves with both electrons, the central carbon is left with only three bonding pairs and no lone pair, that is a sextet of six valence electrons. Three electron pairs and no lone pair means \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridisation, so the three \(\mathrm{C-CH_3}\) bonds lie in one plane with bond angles of about \(120^\circ\), and the unhybridised \(\mathrm{p_z}\) orbital, which is **empty**, stands perpendicular to that plane.

The carbon has therefore changed from \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) tetrahedral in tert-butyl bromide to \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) trigonal planar in the cation. That empty p orbital is what lets the nine \(\alpha\)-hydrogens of the three methyl groups stabilise the cation by hyperconjugation, which is why a tertiary carbocation forms so much more readily than a primary one.
